analysis.one_liner: Bars federal money from backing overseas coal, oil, and gas projects through export agencies and the World Bank.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut off federal financing of overseas fossil fuel projects was introduced in the House in October 2019, referred to three committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SADD Act would stop federal agencies and international financial institutions like the World Bank from using U.S. money to support overseas fossil fuel projects—mines, pipelines, refineries, and power plants that burn coal, oil, or gas. It would rescind unspent funds already set aside for such projects and block future funding to the Export-Import Bank, the Development Finance Corporation, and international lenders until Treasury certified they had policies barring fossil fuel projects. It died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in the United States and abroad, who would stop subsidizing fossil fuel development overseas through their tax dollars and see public financing shift away from the fuels driving climate change and local pollution near foreign project sites.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near overseas fossil projects

how_it_helps.text: It rescinds unobligated federal funds for fossil fuel projects at the Export-Import Bank, the Trade and Development Agency, and the International Development Finance Corporation, and blocks future funds to those agencies and to the World Bank and other international financial institutions unless Treasury certifies they have policies barring fossil fuel projects.

It defines covered projects broadly—any project to extract, refine, produce, transport, or generate power from coal, oil, or natural gas—so the restriction reaches pipelines, terminals, and power plants, not just mines.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel companies and U.S. energy exporters that rely on Export-Import Bank and Development Finance Corporation backing for overseas projects, plus international lenders' fossil fuel lending arms.

drawbacks.text: Rescinding unobligated balances and conditioning future U.S. contributions to international lending institutions could reduce U.S. leverage in those institutions, and critics of similar restrictions argue developing-country energy needs still require financing that fossil fuel projects sometimes supply most cheaply.

Restricting Export-Import Bank and Development Finance Corporation support could cost U.S. companies that export energy equipment and services, and shift foreign energy construction toward competing countries that face no such restriction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending taxpayer support for overseas fossil fuel projects—was real but modest, since U.S. agencies' international fossil fuel financing is a small share of the federal budget, and the bill's main value was symbolic and preventive. The costs it acknowledged (lost overseas contracts for U.S. energy exporters and shifted energy financing abroad) were real but smaller than the public-health and climate costs of continuing those projects. It never received consideration, so the tradeoff was never debated on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees, none of which acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: H.R. 4961 was introduced on October 31, 2019 by Rep. Jared Huffman with two cosponsors, and was referred to the House Appropriations, Financial Services, and Foreign Affairs Committees.
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill moving past committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. agencies and the international fossil fuel industry keep the ability to use public financing for overseas coal, oil, and gas projects, which was the practice the bill would have stopped.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel exporters and their public financiers

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block federal financing of international fossil fuel projects.

for.name: Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Nanette Barragán

against.name: House Financial Services, Appropriations, and Foreign Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without hearings, a markup, or a report for the remaining fourteen months of the Congress.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry and export-finance interests
against.role: Export credit and fossil fuel beneficiaries
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on U.S. export financing of overseas fossil fuel projects during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by three House Democrats with no Republican cosponsors, and no vote ever occurred to reveal a fuller breakdown.

industries.industry: International fossil fuel developers and exporters (oil, gas, coal)
industries.note: The bill would cut off U.S. taxpayer-backed financing through the Export-Import Bank, the Development Finance Corporation, and the Trade and Development Agency for overseas projects to extract, move, or burn fossil fuels. These public backstops lower financing costs for the industry.

industries.industry: International financial institutions receiving U.S. contributions (World Bank, other IFIs)
industries.note: Future U.S. payments would be withheld until Treasury certifies the institution bars fossil fuel projects, tying the flow of public money to a clean-energy standard.
By removing subsidized fossil fuel competition in developing-country energy markets, the bill would advantage cleaner energy projects seeking international public financing.
